title: Data Center Physical Security Checklist: What to Ask Software Vendors
summary: A data center security checklist for your shortlist: seven questions on doors, alarms, racks, GSOC views and privacy by design, ready for every vendor.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR**


A data center physical security checklist asks how a software platform, the layer that interprets what cameras and access control report, handles moments such as a door alarm, a second person at a secure door or a building alarm, and how it is secured and what hardware it needs. Its seven questions score any vendor, and the final section answers them for one platform.


One proposal for a physical security software platform on a data center shortlist usually gets read three times, by three people looking for different things. The security lead reads about doors and racks, the CISO sees one more networked system on the estate, and procurement looks for what it will have to buy. The platform all three are reading about is a layer that interprets what cameras, badge readers and building alarms report and brings an operator the scene behind what it finds.


Two differences separate one platform from another. The first shows up early, because some platforms run on the cameras and access control a site already owns while others need new cameras, which turns a software purchase into a hardware project. The second is what each platform does with the signals those systems produce when something happens at a door, at a rack or in a hall, and each of those moments can be put to every vendor as a question.


## What Should a Data Center Physical Security Checklist Include?


A data center physical security checklist should ask how a software platform handles door alarms, entry at secure doors, activity at the rack, building alarms and the view across many sites, and how the platform is secured and fits what is already installed. Because each question follows something that happens on a data center floor, the seven work as data center physical security evaluation criteria for any vendor:


1. **Does the platform validate a door alarm against the door camera's video in real time, before an operator sees it?**
2. **Can the platform show tailgating at mantraps, turnstiles and secure doors?**
3. **Does the platform alert on hands-on activity at a rack a camera covers?**
4. **Do fire, high-temperature and power alarms reach the security operator with the nearby camera view?**
5. **Can one Global Security Operations Center (GSOC) run every site from one view?**
6. **Does the platform run on existing cameras and access control, and leave the Video Management System (VMS) choice to you?**
7. **What can the vendor show your CISO about security and privacy by design?**


Where the usual data center security checklist asks whether a facility has cameras and badge readers, this one asks what a software platform does with them. Our[overview of what traditional data center security systems miss](https://www.ambient.ai/blog/data-center-physical-security-gaps) covers the gaps behind these questions.


## At the Door, the Test Is What the Operator Receives


Our[reference on entry hardware and access zones](https://www.ambient.ai/learn/data-center-access-control) covers the controls themselves, and these questions begin where they raise a signal.


**1. When a door alarm fires, does the platform reason over the video from the camera at that door in real time and validate the alarm before an operator sees it?** Callup, where the operator pulls up the door's camera after the alarm fires and works out what happened from the footage, is the baseline to measure every answer against. In a data hall, a door propped for a cart of equipment raises the same alarm as one held for any other reason, so ask the vendor to replay a routine held-door alarm being cleared beside one that holds up, and to show the scene that reached the operator with the second.


**2. At mantraps, turnstiles and secure doors, can the platform show two people passing on one badge grant?** Tailgating, also called piggybacking, puts a second person into a secure data hall on someone else's grant. Ask the vendor which doors it covers and what it needs at each one, then have it show what an operator receives. Our post on[how tailgating plays out in a colocation building](https://www.ambient.ai/blog/colocation-physical-security) goes deeper.


## Past the Door, the Same Test Applies at the Rack, in the Hall and Across Every Site


Picture one night shift: a cabinet opens in one aisle and a temperature alarm fires two rows away, while the operators watching sit two time zones away.


**3. On a rack a camera covers, does the platform alert on hands-on activity and send the scene?** The UK's NPSA and NCSC put the rack on the list in their[key considerations for data centre users](https://www.npsa.gov.uk/system/files/documents/NPSA%20Data%20Centre%20Security%20-%20Key%20Considerations%20for%20Users.pdf) : "As well as access control, data centre users should consider access screening processes, intrusion detection such as CCTV, rack security, and asset destruction." Ask the vendor what camera view each rack needs, a placement question our post on[what happens at the rack once a cabinet opens](https://www.ambient.ai/blog/data-center-rack-security) treats in detail.


**4. Do fire, high-temperature and power alarms reach the security operator alongside door alarms, with what the nearest camera shows?** On that night shift, as in any data hall, a high-temperature or power alarm is an operational and a security moment at once, and whoever decides whether to send someone needs the space in view. Ask the vendor which building alarms reach the security view and what the operator sees beside them.


**5. Can one GSOC manage every site from a single view and delegate sites to operators, without a workstation at each site?** The operators two time zones away are the GSOC, and their portfolio grows site by site as[the AI buildout keeps adding new sites](https://www.ambient.ai/blog/hyperscale-data-center-physical-security) . Ask the vendor to hand a site to an operator in the demonstration, then pull up that operator's record.


## The CISO and Procurement Review the Platform as Infrastructure


By the second meeting, the CISO often wants a network diagram and procurement a list of what must be bought.


**6. Does the platform run on the cameras and access control the site already has, and leave the VMS decision to you?** Most estates mix camera models across halls and sites, so the answer decides whether this stays a software purchase. Ask the vendor which camera standards it supports, whether it will confirm coverage on a sample of your own cameras before contract, and whether you can keep your current VMS.


**7. What can the vendor show your CISO about how the platform is secured and protects privacy by design?** The Interagency Security Committee's[best practice on security convergence](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-08/Security%20Convergence%20-%20Achieving%20Integrated%20Security%202022%20Edition.final_.pdf) , US federal guidance for federal facilities, notes that networked security devices expand "the potential attack surface of facilities," so the CISO reviews the platform like any other networked system. Ask for written answers on:


- Encryption at rest, in transit and for live streams.
- What leaves the site.
- Firewall exceptions or open ports.
- Edge device patching and key management.
- How detection treats faces and personal data.
- Customer control of video retention and deletion.
- How system access is controlled and recorded.


## How Ambient.ai Answers the Checklist


Ambient.ai is an[Agentic Physical Security](https://www.ambient.ai/agentic-physical-security) platform whose reasoning Vision-Language Model (VLM), purpose-built for physical security, reads what a camera shows at a door or a rack and, where access control is connected, the scene behind a door or building alarm. Its alerts come from pre-trained threat signatures, the behaviors the model already knows how to recognize, and each alert arrives with the scene attached and leaves the decision with the team.


- **Door alarms validated in real time.** Where access control is connected, Ambient.ai[validates each door forced open or door held open alarm](https://www.ambient.ai/products/ambient-access-intelligence) against what the camera at that door shows, in real time and before it reaches an operator. Where access control is connected, one of those alarms whose video shows something routine, such as a person leaving, is cleared automatically, and one that holds up arrives as an alert with a clip, live video and the floor plan in one view, with no callup needed, for the operator's decision.
- **Tailgating at secure doors.** Where access control is connected, Ambient.ai pairs door events with video for tailgating too, reading each badge grant at a secure door, mantraps included, with the camera view over it, and a pre-trained threat signature alerts when a second person follows the first through on that one grant.
- **Hands-on activity at the rack.** On a rack a camera covers, a[threat signature for hands-on interaction](https://www.ambient.ai/products/ambient-threat-detection) alerts with the scene, so the team can weigh it against the work it knows about, and it performs best where that camera has a clear, close view of one rack.
- **Building alarms with the camera view.** Where access control is connected and carries those inputs, fire, high-temperature and power alarms reach the operator in the same view as door alarms with the nearby camera view beside them, and for a fire or high-temperature alarm that view shows whether anyone is present or leaving. The sensors that raise them remain the foundation, and Ambient.ai adds the scene beside their signal.
- **One view for the GSOC.** Every connected site sits in one browser-based view on any device, with sites delegated to operators, role-based access, single sign-on (SSO) and an audit log, so a GSOC lead can hand each new site to an operator and later see what that operator did.
- **Existing cameras and the VMS choice.** Ambient.ai[connects to standard ONVIF and RTSP cameras](https://www.ambient.ai/integration) through an edge appliance after a pre-deployment compatibility check confirms coverage, and a team can keep its VMS or[consolidate onto the Ambient.ai platform](https://www.ambient.ai/ai-native-video-management) , whichever suits its estate.
- **Security and privacy by design.** For the CISO's network diagram, anonymized metadata rather than raw video leaves the site, and no firewall exceptions are needed. Data is encrypted at rest with AES-256 and in transit with TLS 1.2 or later, live streams use SRTP, edge appliances are patched over the air and keys rotate automatically. Detection uses no facial recognition or personally identifiable information (PII), the customer controls video retention and deletion and has audit visibility into every access to the system, and Ambient.ai operates SOC 2 Type II certified processes.


That opening proposal still has three readers, so put the same seven questions to every vendor on the shortlist and set the answers side by side. The same thinking runs through Ambient.ai's work on[securing data centers](https://www.ambient.ai/solutions/data-centers) . A shortlist built on these questions shows each of those readers how a platform would handle the night a cabinet opens in one aisle, a temperature alarm fires two rows away and the operators who must decide sit in a GSOC far from both.
